To: Bilal Rahman
From: Marta Kowalczyk, Volunteer Coordinator
Subject: Your shift on Saturday, October 11

Dear Bilal,

Thank you for signing up to help at the Millbrook Food Bank. I am writing to confirm your shift this Saturday, October 11, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. You will be sorting donated cans and packing boxes with two other volunteers.

Please come to the side entrance on Tanner Street, not the main door, and arrive ten minutes early so that I can show you around. Wear closed shoes; we will give you gloves and an apron. There is no parking at the building, but bus 14 stops right outside.

If you cannot come, please call me by Friday noon so that I can find a replacement.

Best regards,
Marta Kowalczyk

router.subject: Social history
router.title: How the Weekend Was Invented
paragraphs: A two-day break at the end of every week feels natural today, yet it is a fairly recent invention. In early industrial Britain, factories ran six days a week, and Sunday was the only day off. Many workers, especially skilled craftsmen who were paid for each item they made, simply stayed away on Monday as well. This unofficial holiday became so common that it earned a nickname: "Saint Monday."

Factory owners disliked the custom because they could never predict how many workers would appear. From the middle of the nineteenth century, some of them proposed a trade: if employees came reliably on Monday, they could leave early on Saturday afternoon. The half-day proved popular, and other businesses soon profited from it. Railway companies sold cheap tickets for Saturday trips to the seaside, and football matches were scheduled for Saturday afternoons.

The full two-day weekend arrived later. In 1926, the carmaker Henry Ford gave his factory workers both Saturday and Sunday off without cutting their pay. His motive was partly commercial: people with free time, he reasoned, would spend more money, including on cars. During the economic crisis of the 1930s, shorter weeks were also seen as a way to share scarce work among more people, and by 1940 the forty-hour week had become the legal standard in the United States.

questions.q: According to the passage, why did factory owners dislike "Saint Monday"?
options: Workers demanded higher pay for coming in on Mondays.
It reduced the number of customers on Saturdays.
The law required factories to open six days a week.
They could not tell how many workers would come in.
questions.why: Paragraph 2: owners 'could never predict how many workers would appear'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about workers who stayed away on "Saint Monday"?
options: They were paid for the day anyway.
They had no official permission to be absent.
They usually worked on Sundays instead.
They were mostly employed by railway companies.
questions.why: Paragraph 1 says Sunday was 'the only day off' and calls Monday an 'unofficial holiday'.

questions.q: Why does the author mention railway tickets and football matches?
options: To explain why workers were too tired to work on Mondays
To show that factory owners also ran other businesses
To give examples of how businesses gained from the free afternoon
To argue that leisure mattered more than work in Britain
questions.why: The two examples directly follow the statement that 'other businesses soon profited from it'.

questions.q: The word "scarce" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: hard to find
poorly paid
physically tiring
strictly controlled
questions.why: Scarce means in short supply: in the crisis there was too little work, so it was shared out.

questions.q: According to the passage, all of the following helped to establish the two-day weekend in the United States EXCEPT
options: a carmaker's decision about his own factories
the idea that free time would increase spending
pressure from companies that sold train tickets
the wish to spread work among more people
questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives Ford's decision, his reasoning about spending, and work-sharing in the 1930s. Railway companies belong to the earlier British half-day in paragraph 2.

upper.subject: Neuroscience
upper.title: Rewiring the Brain
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, scientists assumed that the adult brain was essentially fixed. Children's brains developed rapidly, the thinking went, but once a person reached adulthood, the wiring was complete and could only decline. Research over the past few decades has overturned this view. The brain, it turns out, keeps reorganizing itself throughout life, a capacity known as neuroplasticity.

A well-known study of London taxi drivers illustrates the idea. To earn a license, drivers there must memorize thousands of streets, a task that takes years. Brain scans showed that part of the hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, was larger in these drivers than in other adults, and the longer they had been driving, the greater the difference. Plasticity also explains why some patients recover abilities after a stroke: with intensive practice, healthy areas can take over tasks once handled by damaged ones.

Yet rewiring is neither effortless nor always beneficial. Connections that are not used grow weaker, so skills fade without practice. The same mechanism can also strengthen unwanted patterns, as when the nervous system "learns" to keep signaling pain after an injury has healed. Nor does every claim made in the name of plasticity deserve trust: commercial "brain-training" games improve performance on the games themselves, but evidence that they sharpen thinking in general remains weak.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why children's brains develop faster than adults' brains
The brain's ability to change throughout life, and its limits
How taxi drivers in London are trained and licensed
New treatments that repair damaged brain cells
questions.why: Paragraph 1 introduces neuroplasticity, paragraph 2 gives evidence for it, and paragraph 3 begins 'Yet rewiring is neither effortless nor always beneficial'.

questions.q: According to the passage, what did the study of taxi drivers find?
options: Drivers with larger brains learned the streets faster.
Drivers forgot the streets soon after they retired.
Most drivers needed several attempts to earn a license.
A region linked to spatial memory was larger in drivers.
questions.why: Paragraph 2: 'part of the hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, was larger in these drivers than in other adults'.

questions.q: The word "overturned" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: disproved
supported
explained
delayed
questions.why: To overturn a view is to show that it is wrong; the next sentence states the opposite of the old belief.

questions.q: What can be inferred about a person who stops playing a musical instrument for many years?
options: The person's hippocampus will grow larger.
The person will be unable to relearn the instrument.
The connections that support the skill will weaken.
The skill will stay the same, since adult brains are fixed.
questions.why: Paragraph 3: 'Connections that are not used grow weaker, so skills fade without practice.'

questions.q: Why does the author mention "brain-training" games?
options: To recommend an inexpensive way of improving one's memory
To illustrate a claim about plasticity that lacks good evidence
To show that adults learn games more slowly than children
To explain how stroke patients practice lost skills
questions.why: The games follow 'Nor does every claim made in the name of plasticity deserve trust'; evidence for a general benefit 'remains weak'.

That sounds doable. When do you need the new version?

router.script: Welcome to the Ellery Theater, and thank you for coming to tonight's student production. Before the lights go down, a few quick reminders. Please switch your phones off completely, because even a silent phone lights up and distracts the actors. Photography isn't allowed during the show, but the cast will be in the lobby afterward and would love to take pictures with you. Tonight's performance runs about ninety minutes, with one fifteen-minute intermission. If you leave your seat during the show, an usher will let you back in at a suitable moment. Thank you, and enjoy the play.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To remind the audience of the rules before a show
To introduce the actors in tonight's play
To announce that the performance will start late
To invite students to join a theater group
questions.why: 'Before the lights go down, a few quick reminders', followed by rules about phones, photographs and leaving one's seat.

questions.q: What does the speaker say about taking photographs?
options: It is allowed if the flash is turned off.
It is permitted only during the intermission.
It will be possible in the lobby after the show.
It must be approved by an usher.
questions.why: 'Photography isn't allowed during the show, but the cast will be in the lobby afterward and would love to take pictures with you.'

router.setting: Listen to an announcement in a classroom.
router.script: Right, I'll let you go in a moment, but first, a quick request. This afternoon you'll get an email with a link to our mid-semester feedback survey. It takes about five minutes, and it's anonymous, so I won't know who wrote what. Now, this isn't the official evaluation you fill in at the end of term. This one comes straight to me, and I use it to adjust the course while you're still taking it. Last year, for instance, students asked for more worked examples, so I added them. The survey closes on Sunday night, and on Monday I'll tell you what I plan to change.

questions.q: What is the professor mainly talking about?
options: The results of last year's final evaluation
A change to the date of the midterm exam
A new rule about emailing the professor
A chance to comment on the course while it is running
questions.why: The mid-semester survey 'comes straight to me, and I use it to adjust the course while you're still taking it'.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention worked examples?
options: To explain what will be on the next test
To show that earlier feedback led to a change
To describe a problem with this year's class
To remind students what to bring on Monday
questions.why: 'Last year, for instance, students asked for more worked examples, so I added them.' It is an example of feedback being used.

router.subject: Botany
router.script: Plants have a problem that animals don't. When something comes along to eat them, they can't run away. So, how does a plant protect itself? Well, the first line of defense is physical. Think of the thorns on a rose, or the tough, waxy surface of a holly leaf. Some leaves are even covered in tiny hairs that make it hard for small insects to walk on them. The second line is chemical. Many plants fill their leaves with substances that taste bitter or are actually poisonous. Caffeine is a good example. We enjoy it in coffee and tea, but the plant makes it to poison insects that chew on its leaves. Now, here's the part I find most impressive. Some plants call for help. When caterpillars start chewing on a corn plant, the damaged leaves release a scent into the air. That scent attracts a certain kind of wasp, and the wasps attack the caterpillars. In other words, the plant is sending out a signal that says, 'Your lunch is over here.' And all of this costs the plant energy, which is why many plants don't produce these chemicals all the time. They wait until they're actually attacked. So next time you walk past a quiet green field, remember, it's not as peaceful as it looks.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why insects prefer some plants to others
Ways in which plants protect themselves from being eaten
How farmers keep caterpillars away from their corn
The effects that caffeine has on the human body
questions.why: The professor asks 'how does a plant protect itself?' and then describes physical, chemical and indirect defenses.

questions.q: According to the professor, why do some plants produce caffeine?
options: To attract insects that carry pollen
To help their leaves hold water
To grow faster in poor soil
To poison insects that feed on them
questions.why: 'The plant makes it to poison insects that chew on its leaves.'

questions.q: What happens when caterpillars chew on a corn plant?
options: The plant gives off a smell that brings wasps.
The plant's leaves grow tiny hairs.
The caterpillars are poisoned by caffeine.
The plant stops producing chemicals.
questions.why: 'The damaged leaves release a scent into the air. That scent attracts a certain kind of wasp, and the wasps attack the caterpillars.'

questions.q: What is the professor's attitude toward plants that "call for help"?
options: She doubts that it has been proved.
She thinks it is less effective than thorns.
She finds it especially remarkable.
She worries that it harms useful insects.
questions.why: She introduces this defense with 'here's the part I find most impressive'.

router.subject: Marketing
router.script: Here's a price tag that every one of you has seen a thousand times. A shirt costs nineteen ninety-nine. Not twenty dollars. Why? It's only one cent. Well, marketers have a name for this: charm pricing. And there are two main reasons it works. The first is the way we read numbers. We read from left to right, and our brain starts judging the price as soon as it sees the first digit. So nineteen ninety-nine gets filed under 'nineteen-something,' not 'twenty.' Researchers call this the left-digit effect. And notice, it only works when the first digit changes. Dropping a price from three sixty to three fifty-nine does almost nothing. The second reason is what a nine signals. Over the years, shoppers have learned to connect prices ending in nine with sales and discounts. In one well-known experiment, a clothing catalog offered the same dress at thirty-four, thirty-nine, and forty-four dollars. Which sold best? The thirty-nine-dollar one. It even beat the cheaper price. Now, does that mean every store should use nines? Not quite. Have a look at the menu in an expensive restaurant, or the price tag on a luxury watch. You'll usually see round numbers there. A round price says quality, and a nine says discount. So the right ending depends on what you want your customers to think.

questions.q: What is the main topic of the talk?
options: How stores decide when to hold sales
Why luxury products cost more to make
Why prices just below a round number affect shoppers
How shoppers calculate discounts in their heads
questions.why: The professor asks why a shirt costs nineteen ninety-nine instead of twenty dollars and gives two reasons that 'charm pricing' works.

questions.q: According to the professor, what is the left-digit effect?
options: People judge a price mainly by its first number.
People remember the last number of a price best.
People read prices more slowly than words.
People prefer prices that have fewer digits.
questions.why: 'Our brain starts judging the price as soon as it sees the first digit.'

questions.q: Why does the professor mention a price change from $3.60 to $3.59?
options: To prove that even a one-cent discount always raises sales
To give an example of the prices used in luxury stores
To explain how the experiment with the dress was designed
To show that the first digit must change for the effect to work
questions.why: 'It only works when the first digit changes. Dropping a price from three sixty to three fifty-nine does almost nothing.'

questions.q: What does the professor imply about an expensive restaurant that used prices ending in ninety-nine?
options: It would sell more meals than before.
It might make its food seem lower in quality.
It would confuse customers who read quickly.
It would have to change its prices more often.
questions.why: 'A round price says quality, and a nine says discount', which is why expensive restaurants use round numbers.

Really? So we have a free hour. What do you want to do?

lower.setting: Listen to an announcement in a supermarket.

Special prices on some food today
A change in opening hours
Free drinks for shoppers

lower.setting: Listen to an announcement in a classroom.

The registrar's office is next to the bank.

options: They are steep. Have you looked into the department grant?
My heart races before every exam, too.
Then I'm glad you signed up in time.

upper.setting: Listen to a conversation between two students.
script: So you're really going to spend the spring in Lisbon? I can't help thinking it's a glorified vacation.
That's a bit harsh. I'll be taking four courses, and two of them are taught in Portuguese.
Sure, but will any of it count toward your degree? My cousin went abroad and ended up graduating a semester late.
I checked. Three of the four transfer. And frankly, there's more to university than ticking boxes.
Easy to say until you see the bill.
The exchange fee's the same as our tuition. It's the flights that sting. Look, I'm not saying it's for everyone, but you might surprise yourself.
Maybe. I'll believe it when I see your transcript.

questions.q: What does the man mean when he calls the semester abroad "a glorified vacation"?
options: He thinks the woman has earned a holiday.
He believes Lisbon is too expensive to live in.
He doubts that it has much academic value.
He wishes that he could travel with her.
questions.why: A 'glorified vacation' is a holiday made to sound more serious than it is; he goes on to ask whether any of it will count toward her degree.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the man at the end of the conversation?
options: He is still not convinced by the woman's arguments.
He has decided to apply for the same program.
He agrees that flights are the biggest problem.
He plans to check the woman's grades for her.
questions.why: 'Maybe. I'll believe it when I see your transcript' shows that he remains skeptical.

upper.setting: Listen to an announcement from a university's graduate school.
upper.script: Attention, all master's and doctoral students who plan to graduate this spring. The Graduate School's final deadline for submitting a thesis is April twenty-fourth, and I should stress that no extensions will be granted. Before you can submit, however, your document must pass a format check, which covers margins, page numbering, and the reference list. That check takes up to five working days, and in our experience roughly half of all theses are sent back for corrections at least once. So, realistically, if you haven't uploaded your draft for checking by the tenth, you're cutting it very fine. The format guidelines are on the Graduate School website.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To announce that a deadline has been extended
To urge students to start a required check early
To explain how a finished thesis will be graded
To introduce new rules for reference lists
questions.why: The speaker explains that the format check takes time and often has to be repeated, and warns students not to leave it until after the tenth.

questions.q: What does the speaker imply about students who upload a draft after the tenth?
options: They will have to pay a late fee.
Their format check will be refused.
They may run out of time for corrections.
They can ask for a short extension.
questions.why: The check takes up to five working days and about half of theses come back for corrections, so later than the tenth is 'cutting it very fine' for a deadline with no extensions.

upper.subject: Astronomy
upper.script: So here's the obvious problem. A black hole, by definition, gives off no light. Its gravity is so strong that nothing that falls in can get back out, not even light itself. So how on earth do you find something you can't see? The short answer is, you watch what it does to its surroundings. One approach is to track stars. At the center of our galaxy, astronomers spent years following a handful of stars that whip around an empty-looking point at tremendous speeds. From those orbits, they worked out that the invisible object must have the mass of about four million suns, packed into a tiny region. Nothing else we know of fits that description. A second clue is X-rays. When a black hole pulls gas off a neighboring star, that gas doesn't drop straight in. It spirals, and as it does, it heats up to millions of degrees and glows in X-rays. And then there's a much more recent method, which, frankly, still gives me goosebumps. In twenty fifteen, detectors picked up gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space itself, produced when two black holes collided more than a billion years ago. So notice the pattern here. In none of these cases are we observing the black hole directly. We're inferring it, the way you'd infer wind from the movement of the trees.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How black holes form when large stars collapse
Why the center of our galaxy contains so many stars
How X-ray telescopes were first developed
How scientists find objects that cannot be seen directly
questions.why: The professor asks 'how on earth do you find something you can't see?' and describes three indirect methods.

questions.q: How did astronomers work out the mass of the object at the center of our galaxy?
options: By studying the orbits of stars near it
By measuring the X-rays coming from it
By counting the stars that had fallen into it
By recording gravitational waves from it
questions.why: 'From those orbits, they worked out that the invisible object must have the mass of about four million suns.'

questions.q: What is the professor's attitude toward the detection of gravitational waves?
options: He considers it unreliable.
He thinks it has been overpraised.
He finds it thrilling.
He regards it as routine.
questions.why: He says the method 'frankly, still gives me goosebumps', an expression of excitement.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention wind and trees?
options: To explain how gas moves around a black hole
To illustrate how an unseen thing is known by its effects
To describe the conditions needed for observation
To suggest that black holes are common in nature
questions.why: 'We're inferring it, the way you'd infer wind from the movement of the trees': wind is invisible, but its effects are not.

upper.subject: Philosophy
upper.script: I want to start today with a ship. According to the ancient writer Plutarch, the people of Athens kept the ship of their hero Theseus for centuries as a kind of monument. Wood rots, of course, so whenever a plank decayed, they swapped in a new one. Now suppose that, in the end, not a single original plank is left. Is it still the ship of Theseus? Hands up if you say yes. Hmm, most of you. OK. Now let me spoil your confidence. In the seventeenth century, Thomas Hobbes added a twist. Suppose somebody had quietly collected every old plank as it was removed, and then put them all back together. Now there are two ships. Which one is the real one? If you think a thing is just its material, you have to pick the rebuilt pile of old wood. If you think what matters is a continuous history, an unbroken story, you'll stay with the ship that was repaired. And notice, this isn't really about boats. Many of the cells in your body have been replaced since you were a child, and yet you'd insist you're the same person. I'm not going to hand you a solution, by the way. Philosophers have been arguing over this one for two thousand years, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you it's settled.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Whether a thing stays the same when its parts change
The methods ancient Athenians used to repair ships
A disagreement between two historians about Theseus
The reasons the cells of the body are replaced
questions.why: The professor asks whether a ship whose planks have all been replaced is 'still the ship of Theseus' and then extends the question.

questions.q: What did Hobbes add to the original story?
options: The claim that the ship had never existed
The idea that the ship was finally lost at sea
The idea that the old planks were rebuilt into a ship
The fact that the new planks were a different wood
questions.why: 'Suppose somebody had quietly collected every old plank as it was removed, and then put them all back together. Now there are two ships.'

questions.q: Why does the professor mention the cells of the human body?
options: To explain why wood decays faster than living tissue
To prove that people become different every few years
To correct a mistake in Plutarch's account
To show that the puzzle also applies to people
questions.why: 'This isn't really about boats': our cells are replaced, 'and yet you'd insist you're the same person'.

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the puzzle?
options: Hobbes solved it in the seventeenth century.
It has no generally accepted answer.
Most students already know the right answer.
Philosophers have lost interest in it.
questions.why: 'Philosophers have been arguing over this one for two thousand years, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you it's settled.'

email.scenario: You are a student who drives to campus. Yesterday you parked in Lot C, where your semester permit allows you to park, and the permit was clearly displayed inside your car. When you returned after class, you found a $40 ticket for parking without a permit. You believe the ticket was given by mistake. You decide to write to Mr. Deng at the Parking Office.
email.subject: Parking ticket given by mistake
bullets: Describe what happened when you parked on campus.
Explain why you think the ticket is a mistake.
Ask Mr. Deng to cancel the ticket.
email.model:
Dear Mr. Deng,

I am writing about a parking ticket that I received yesterday, March 12. I parked my car in Lot C at about 9:30 a.m. and went to my classes. When I came back at 2:00 p.m., I found ticket number 30417 under the wiper. It says that I parked without a permit.

I believe this is a mistake. I bought a semester permit for Lot C in January, and it was hanging from the mirror, where it always is. I have attached a photo of the permit, which I took as soon as I found the ticket, and a copy of my payment receipt.

Could you please check your records and cancel the ticket? If you need any other information, or if I should bring the permit to your office, please let me know.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
Gabriela Montoya

professor.name: Dr. Estrada
professor.post: This week we are studying how citizens take part in elections. In most democracies, voting is a choice, and in some elections fewer than half of the people who are allowed to vote actually do so. A number of countries, including Australia and Belgium, take a different approach: citizens are required by law to vote, and those who do not may have to pay a small fine. What is your view? Should voting in national elections be compulsory? Why or why not?

students.name: Nikolai
students.post: I support compulsory voting. When everyone has to vote, the result reflects the whole population, not just the people who are most interested in politics or who have time to go. Leaders then have to pay attention to every group, including young people and those with low incomes, who often stay home.

students.name: Zainab
students.post: I disagree. In my opinion, the right to vote includes the right not to vote. If people are forced to go, many will choose without knowing anything about the candidates, just to avoid a fine. I think it is better to make voting easier, for example by letting people vote by mail or on a weekend.

discussion.model: I believe that voting should remain voluntary, although I understand Nikolai's point that a higher turnout makes a result more representative. As Zainab says, a vote that is cast only to avoid a fine is not a real opinion, and it may even make the result less meaningful. I would add another reason: a law is only useful if it can be enforced fairly. Checking millions of citizens and collecting small fines costs money, and the people who are fined are often those who had the most difficulty reaching a polling place. Instead of punishing people, governments should remove the obstacles that keep them away. Election day could be a public holiday, registration could be automatic, and schools could teach students how elections work. If voting is convenient and people understand why it matters, most of them will take part without being forced.

repeat.scenario: You are learning how to assist the teacher of a cooking class. Listen to the teacher and repeat what she says. Repeat only once.
repeat.picture: A teaching kitchen with six cooking stations, aprons hanging by the door and an oven with a timer.
sentences: Today we are baking fresh bread rolls.
Every student needs a clean apron.

Before the students go home, check that every stove is off and that the floor has been swept.

interview.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about volunteering and community. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.q: Thanks for making time for this interview. First, I'd like to hear about your own experience. Please tell me about a time when you helped someone in your community or took part in a volunteer activity. What did you do, and how did you feel afterward?
questions.model: Last spring, I took part in a clean-up day along the river near my home. A local group organized it, and about thirty people came. We spent the morning picking up plastic bottles and old bags, and my job was to sort what could be recycled. It was harder than I expected, because it was hot and my back hurt after two hours. But afterward I felt proud. When I walked along the river the next week, the path looked completely different, and I knew I had helped a little. I also met two neighbors that I had never spoken to before, and we still greet each other.

questions.q: Some people like to volunteer as part of a large, organized group, while others prefer to help in small, informal ways, such as assisting a neighbor. Which do you prefer, and why?
questions.model: I prefer to help in small, informal ways. The main reason is my schedule. I study during the day and work some evenings, so I cannot promise to be somewhere every Saturday morning. But I can carry shopping for the older woman who lives next door, or help my friend's younger brother with his math homework when I have a free hour. I also like that I can see the result immediately and that I know the person I am helping. Large organizations do important work, of course, and maybe I will join one when my hours are more regular. For now, small things suit me better.

questions.q: Let's turn to your opinion now. It is sometimes said that volunteering mainly benefits the volunteer, for example because it looks good on a job application, rather than the community. Do you agree? Why or why not?
questions.model: I don't really agree. It is true that some people volunteer because they want something to write on a job application, and we should not pretend otherwise. But the community still benefits. If someone spends a Saturday serving meals, the people who eat those meals are helped, whatever the reason was. In addition, people often start for selfish reasons and continue for better ones. A friend of mine began tutoring children because her scholarship required it, and two years later she is still doing it because she enjoys it. So in my view, the motive matters much less than the work that actually gets done.

questions.q: Here is my last question. In many towns, volunteers do jobs such as cleaning parks or running the local library. Should work like this be left to volunteers, or should local governments pay people to do it? Why?
questions.model: I think it should be a mix of both. Basic services, like collecting trash and keeping parks safe, are the government's job, and people already pay taxes for them. If a town depends on volunteers for essential work, the richer neighborhoods, where people have more free time, will end up cleaner than the poorer ones, and that is not fair. However, volunteers can add something extra. For example, residents can plant flowers, paint a wall, or organize a street party, and these activities also help neighbors get to know each other. So the town should guarantee the basics and then support volunteers with tools and small grants instead of replacing them.
